CS::Complexity.b: An asymptotic upper bound: \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) if there are constants \(C, n_0\) with \(f(n) \leq C\,g(n)\) for all \(n \geq n_0\). It says nothing about a lower bound, and it says nothing for the specific inputs you happen to have.

CS::Complexity.f: Why is big-O a poor predictor of real speed?
CS::Complexity.b: It ignores constants, and in practice constants dominate. Insertion sort is \(O(n^2)\) and merge sort \(O(n\log n)\), yet for \(n\) under about 20 insertion sort wins because of cache behaviour and low overhead. Use \(\Theta\) when you care about the true growth.

| class | shape | example |
||---|---|---|
| \(O(1)\) | constant | array index, hash lookup |
| \(O(\log n)\) | logarithmic | binary search, balanced-tree descent |
| \(O(n)\) | linear | scan |
| \(O(n\log n)\) | sorting | merge sort, heap sort |
| \(O(n^2)\) | quadratic | bubble sort, naive all-pairs |
| \(O(2^n)\), \(O(n!)\) | exponential, factorial | exhaustive search, TSP |

CS::Complexity.f: What is a P versus NP problem?
CS::Complexity.b: P is the set of decision problems solvable in polynomial time. NP is the set whose solutions are verifiable in polynomial time. \(P \stackrel{?}{=} NP\) asks whether every easily verified problem is also easily solved. It is a question about verifiability versus findability.

CS::Complexity.f: What is NP-hardness, and why is it the right notion of hard?
CS::Complexity.b: A problem is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time, so a fast solver for it would collapse the hierarchy. It is the standard certificate of intractability, and it is what makes SAT, travelling salesman and knapsack hard.

CS::Complexity.f: How do you show a problem is NP-hard?
CS::Complexity.b: By exhibiting a polynomial-time reduction from a known NP-hard problem, and proving both directions of the equivalence. Restating the problem in different words is not a proof, and exponential-looking brute force is not evidence of hardness.

CS::Complexity.f: What is space complexity, and why does it surprise people?
CS::Complexity.b: Space is the memory a computation needs, and a naive reading suggests more memory is always worse. But any \(O(n^2)\)-time algorithm can be made to run in \(O(\log n)\) space by recomputing, and any polynomial-space problem has an exponential-time algorithm, so the two measures are not simply ordered.

CS::Algorithms.f: When is divide and conquer appropriate?
CS::Algorithms.b: When the problem splits into independent subproblems of smaller size, and combining their solutions is cheap. The recurrence is \(T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)\), and the Master theorem reads off the result. Non-independent subproblems mean you need dynamic programming.

For \(T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(n^d)\), with \(a \geq 1, b > 1\):
• \(d > \log_b a \): \(T(n) = O(n^d)\) -- the work at the leaves dominates.
• \(d = \log_b a \): \(T(n) = O(n^d \log n)\).
• \(d < \log_b a \): \(T(n) = O(n^{\log_b a})\) -- recursion dominates.
Merge sort is the classic borderline case.

CS::Algorithms.f: What does the Master theorem not cover?
CS::Algorithms.b: Recurrences with subtraction, with irregular branching, or with \(f(n) = O(n^d \log^k n)\). Also \(T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)\) (merge sort) is exactly borderline and needs the logarithmic factor, which a careless reading misses.

Only when the locally best choice is provably extendable to a global optimum, which is certified by the exchange argument or stays-ahead. Interval scheduling, Huffman coding and MST are greedy and correct; most interval-scheduling-looking problems with weights are not.

CS::Algorithms.f: What is dynamic programming good for?
CS::Algorithms.b: Overlapping subproblems plus an optimal substructure, where a table of smaller answers can be reused. Longest common subsequence, shortest paths, knapsack, optimal BST. The cost is usually polynomial space, and the win comes from reuse.

CS::Algorithms.f: What is the difference between recursion and dynamic programming?
CS::Algorithms.b: Recursion re-solves the same subproblem many times, e.g. naive Fibonacci in \(O(\varphi^n)\) with an exponential call tree. Memoising or bottom-up tabulation makes it linear. The structure is identical; only the reuse differs.

CS::Algorithms.f: What is the 0/1 knapsack recurrence, and why is it 0/1?
CS::Algorithms.b:
\[ dp[i][w] = \max\big(dp[i-1][w],\; v_i + dp[i-1][w-w_i]\big) \]
The \(i-1\) index forces each item to be used at most once. Unbounded knapsack instead uses \(dp[w]\) on both sides, which allows repeats. Cost is \(O(nW)\), pseudo-polynomial in the capacity.

Because \(O(nW)\) is polynomial in the numeric value of \(W\), but \(W\) may be encoded in \(\log W\) bits, so in the input size it is exponential. Knapsack is therefore only weakly NP-complete, and is exactly where dynamic programming and a greedy-like approach can still be useful.

CS::Algorithms.f: How does Dijkstra's algorithm work, and what is its limitation?
CS::Algorithms.b: Repeatedly finalises the closest unvisited vertex, relaxing its edges: \(O((V+E)\log V)\) with a binary heap. It requires non-negative edge weights. With negative edges a closer vertex may still improve later, and the algorithm silently gives wrong answers; use Bellman-Ford (no negativity needed) when weights may be negative.

A* is Dijkstra guided by an admissible heuristic \(h\): \[ f(n) = g(n) + h(n) \]
Admissible means \(h\) never overestimates the true remaining cost, which guarantees optimality. With \(h=0\) it reduces to Dijkstra, so A* is a generalisation.

CS::Algorithms.f: What is memoization versus bottom-up tabulation?
CS::Algorithms.b: Memoization adds caching to top-down recursion, computing only reachable states. Bottom-up fills a table in dependency order, computing all states but with no recursion overhead and no stack risk. They produce the same table; the choice is recursion depth versus wasted work.

CS::DataStructures.f: Compare array, linked list, and dynamic array.
CS::DataStructures.b:
| structure | random access | insert at front | memory |
||---|---|---|---|
| static array | \(O(1)\) | \(O(n)\) | contiguous, no pointers |
| linked list | \(O(n)\) | \(O(1)\) given a cursor | scattered, per-node overhead |
| dynamic array | \(O(1)\) | \(O(n)\) | contiguous, amortised \(O(1)\) append |
In practice dynamic arrays win almost everywhere because of cache locality.

CS::DataStructures.f: Why is dynamic-array append amortised O(1)?
CS::DataStructures.b: On reaching capacity, double it and copy. A run of \(n\) appends performs \(O(\log n)\) resizes totalling \(1+2+4+\dots < 2n\) copies, so the cost is \(O(n)\) over \(n\) operations. Growth by a constant factor instead would make append \(O(n)\) amortised in the worst case.

CS::DataStructures.f: What is the invariant of a binary heap?
CS::DataStructures.b: Every node is at least as large as its children (max-heap), so the maximum is always at the root. It gives \(O(1)\) find-max, \(O(\log n)\) insert and remove-max, and the linear-time heapify (\(\Theta(n)\), from the last internal node downwards) needed to build from an array.

CS::DataStructures.f: How good is a hash table, and what is the weak point?
CS::DataStructures.b: Average \(O(1)\) insert, lookup and delete, but worst case \(O(n)\) when every key collides. Adversarial keys can force this, so production tables randomise the hash. Also load factor above about 0.7 degrades linearly, and iteration order is unordered.

CS::DataStructures.f: What is a B-tree and why do databases use it?
CS::DataStructures.b: A balanced tree with many keys per node, so it is very shallow. A node sized to a 16 KB disk page holds about 1000 keys, so the fanout is ~1000: depth 2 stores about \(10^6\) keys and depth 3 about \(10^9\). A binary search tree would need depth 20 and \(20\) random reads for the same \(10^6\) keys. The node size is chosen to match the disk page, which is why the structure is disk-friendly.

CS::DataStructures.f: What is a B-tree versus a B+ tree?
CS::DataStructures.b: A B+ tree stores data only in leaves and links them in order, so range scans are a simple sequential walk. A B tree stores data in every node, gaining one level of capacity but losing ordered-leaf scanning. Databases mostly use B+ trees.

CS::DataStructures.f: What are the trade-offs of quicksort?
CS::DataStructures.b: In-place and \(O(n\log n)\) on average with excellent cache behaviour, but \(O(n^2)\) on sorted or reverse-sorted input with a naive pivot. Median-of-three or introsort (which switches to heapsort when recursion gets too deep) removes the worst case. Mergesort is stable and \(O(n\log n)\) worst case but needs \(O(n)\) extra space.

CS::DataStructures.f: What is a graph adjacency list versus adjacency matrix?
CS::DataStructures.b: Adjacency list is \(O(V+E)\) space and takes \(O(\deg(v))\) to list neighbours, so it is the right choice for sparse graphs (almost all real ones). A matrix is \(O(V^2)\) space but gives \(O(1)\) edge lookup, which only pays off for dense graphs or repeated membership tests.

CS::PL.f: What is the difference between a compiled and interpreted language?
CS::PL.b: Compilation translates the whole program before running, so errors surface early and loops can be optimised; interpretation executes statement by statement, so it starts instantly and is easy to debug. Most modern languages are hybrid: e.g. V8 compiles JS to bytecode, JIT-compiles hot functions, and Java bytecode is interpreted or JIT-compiled per method.

CS::PL.f: What is the difference between statically and dynamically typed languages?
CS::PL.b: Static types are checked before running, and types are part of the program, so they are documented and refactorable. Dynamic types defer to runtime, giving flexibility. Note that static typing does not prevent memory unsafety: C is statically typed and has buffer overflows, because type safety and memory safety are different properties.

Guaranteeing that a program never dereferences an invalid or freed pointer, and that memory is freed exactly once. Rust gets it from ownership and borrowing checked at compile time; garbage-collected languages get it from a tracing collector; C and C++ do not, which is why use-after-free and buffer overflow account for a large share of security vulnerabilities.

CS::PL.f: What is manual memory management's core difficulty?
CS::PL.b: Every allocation must be matched by exactly one free, on every path including errors, exceptions and early returns. A leak is a missed free; a double free is two; a use-after-free is reading memory that has been handed back. The three failures are one bookkeeping bug seen three ways.

CS::PL.f: What is the difference between heap and stack allocation?
CS::PL.b: The stack holds locals and return addresses, is freed automatically on return, and is fast but small and LIFO. The heap is for dynamically sized objects, lives until explicitly freed or garbage-collected, and is larger. Allocating a large array on the stack is a real bug: it can smash the stack rather than growing it.

CS::PL.f: What is the difference between pass-by-value, pass-by-reference, and pass-by-pointer?
CS::PL.b: Pass-by-value copies, so the callee cannot affect the caller's variable. Pass-by-reference passes an alias, so it can. Pass-by-pointer passes an address explicitly, so \(nullptr\) is possible and the callee can reassign the pointer. The commonest bug is expecting pass-by-value semantics and being surprised that the caller sees no change.

CS::PL.f: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class?
CS::PL.b: An interface specifies capabilities with no state; an abstract class may hold state and provide implementations. So multiple interfaces can be combined but only one class can be inherited from. The distinction is a design signal, not just syntax: use interfaces to describe roles, abstract classes to share implementation.

CS::OS.f: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
CS::OS.b: A process is an address space plus resources; a thread is a stack and registers inside a process. Threads in one process share memory, so communication is cheap but a data race in one corrupts all. Processes are isolated, so a crash is contained but communication needs pipes or shared memory.

CS::OS.f: What is context switching, and why is it expensive?
CS::OS.b: Saving one thread's registers, stack pointer and program counter, then loading another's. The cost is the bookkeeping plus cache and TLB pollution: the new thread runs against cold caches, which usually dominates. This is why reducing switches matters more than making them cheaper.

Behaviour that depends on the unsynchronised interleaving of concurrent operations, so the result is not deterministic. Classic form: check-then-act, e.g. testing a counter, then incrementing it non-atomically. Fixes are mutual exclusion, atomics, or immutable data that removes the window.

CS::OS.f: What is the difference between a mutex and a semaphore?
CS::OS.b: A mutex is mutual exclusion: one owner at a time, and only the owner may release. A semaphore is a counter of N permits with no ownership, so it can signal a different thread and can be used to count N resources. Using a semaphore of one as a lock is a common but lossy substitution, since release-by-another is then allowed.

CS::OS.f: What is a deadlock, and what are the four conditions?
CS::OS.b:
Two or more threads each waiting on the other, permanently blocked.
1. Mutual exclusion: a resource is held exclusively.
2. Hold and wait: a thread holds while requesting more.
3. No preemption: resources cannot be forcibly taken.
4. Circular wait: the wait-for graph has a cycle.
Break any one to prevent it, and the standard orderings (global lock order, or try-lock) target the last.

CS::OS.f: What is a memory barrier, and when is it needed?
CS::OS.b: A fence that forbids the compiler or CPU from reordering or caching writes across it. It is needed for lock-free code publishing data: without a release barrier the data write can become visible after the flag write, so a reader can see the flag but not the data. An ordinary mutex implies the needed barriers, so you rarely write them yourself.

Giving each process its own address space and mapping it to physical frames on demand. It gives isolation, lets programs exceed physical memory via paging, and simplifies loading. The price is a page table (and TLB misses) plus the possibility of thrashing when working sets exceed physical memory.

Paging moves individual pages between RAM and disk as needed, so a process needs only its active pages resident; the virtual address space never has to fit anywhere whole. Swapping moves a whole process. Paging won, and "swapping" in modern systems usually means reclaiming anonymous pages rather than whole processes.

CS::OS.f: What is a file system journal?
CS::OS.b: A log of intended metadata operations, written before they are applied, so a crash mid-update can be replayed or rolled back. It protects metadata only: after replay the directory structure is consistent, but a partially written file's contents are still whatever was flushed. ext4 and NTFS are journalling; FAT is not.

CS::Networking.f: Where does each layer sit, and what does each do?
CS::Networking.b: Bottom to top: physical (bits, voltage), data link (frames, MAC, per-hop), network (packets, IP routing), transport (ports, reliability, TCP/UDP), application (HTTP, DNS, SMTP). Each layer adds a header and offers its service to the one above, using the services of the one below.

CS::Networking.f: Why is TCP called end-to-end reliable, and what is its cost?
CS::Networking.b: Because reliability is implemented in the hosts, not in routers, so it works across any unreliable path. The cost is latency, head-of-line blocking, and the handshake plus acknowledgement traffic. It also means the network core can drop or reorder packets without breaking correctness, which is why NAT and firewalls can be stateless.

CS::Networking.f: What is the three-way handshake, and why not two?
CS::Networking.b:
1. Client sends SYN.
2. Server replies SYN+ACK.
3. Client sends ACK.
Two messages would leave an ambiguity: a delayed first SYN could make the server keep a half-open connection it will never hear about. The third message confirms both sides agree, which is also what lets the client report its initial receive window.

CS::Networking.f: What causes the Nagle algorithm to hurt latency?
CS::Networking.b: Nagle withholds a small segment until an in-flight one is acknowledged, to avoid wasting bandwidth. Combined with delayed ACK it can add hundreds of milliseconds to interactive traffic. Modern stacks often set both off (TCP_NODELAY) and rely on application-level batching instead.

CS::Networking.f: What is a subnet mask for, and how do you tell network from host bits?
CS::Networking.b: It marks which part of an IP address identifies the network and which the host, so a router knows what to forward. The host part is not all zeros (this network) or all ones (broadcast). CIDR \(192.168.1.0/24\) gives 24 network bits and 8 host bits, so 254 usable addresses.

CS::Networking.f: What is a DNS record, and how does resolution work?
CS::Networking.b: Names map to records. A resolver walks the hierarchy: root, then TLD, then authoritative nameserver, using referrals plus recursion, and caches the answer with a TTL. Records you meet in practice: A/AAAA for addresses, CNAME for aliases, MX for mail, TXT for verification and policy, NS for delegation.

CS::Networking.f: What is congestion control, and what is it trying to do?
CS::Networking.b: Adjust the sending rate to keep the network just below capacity, without central knowledge. Reno and CUBIC grow the window until packet loss or delay signals congestion, then halve it; BBR instead uses delay and throughput as signals. It is a control problem run in the endpoints, so it has to be conservative.

CS::Databases.b:
Atomicity: all or nothing, via rollback.
Consistency: constraints hold at commit.
Isolation: concurrent transactions behave as if serial.
Durability: committed data survives a crash.
Durability costs a write to stable storage on every commit; isolation costs concurrency.

Read uncommitted can see dirty data; read committed prevents that but can re-read a different value in one transaction; repeatable read prevents that but can show phantoms; serializable prevents phantoms too, at the greatest cost. The levels are ordered by anomalies prevented, and higher levels buy correctness with locks or multi-version concurrency control.

CS::Databases.f: What do the normal forms fix, and what is the point of 3NF?
CS::Databases.b: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: no partial dependency on a composite key. 3NF: no transitive dependency of non-key attributes on the key. The goal is not tidiness but that each fact is stored once, which is what makes anomalies (update, insertion, deletion) impossible rather than merely handled.

CS::Databases.f: Why does an index help, and when does it not?
CS::Databases.b: B-trees let a lookup skip most rows, turning \(O(n)\) scans into \(O(\log n)\) plus a random read. It does not help when the predicate is not selective, when it is applied to a function of the column, or on small tables where a sequential scan wins. Every index also costs write amplification and space.

CS::Databases.f: What is a database index, and what are the two main kinds?
CS::Databases.b: A redundant structure mapping column values to row locations, maintained on write. B-tree for range and equality, compact and log-structured. Hash for equality only, constant time but no ordering. The planner picks based on the query.

CS::Databases.f: What is write-ahead logging, and why is it correct?
CS::Databases.b: Log the changes before they are applied to the data pages, so after a crash you replay the log to reach a consistent state. It is correct because the log is ordered, and because replaying a prefix of committed operations cannot lose a committed transaction.

CS::Security.f: What is the difference between symmetric and public-key cryptography?
CS::Security.b: Symmetric uses one shared secret for both directions and is fast, but key distribution is the hard part. Public-key uses a mathematically linked pair: a private key you keep and a public key you publish, so no shared secret has to be delivered. In practice TLS and SSH use both: public-key to establish a secret, symmetric for the data.

CS::Security.f: What properties does a hash need for cryptographic use?
CS::Security.b: Preimage resistance, second-preimage resistance, and collision resistance. MD5 was collision-broken in 2004 and SHA-1 in 2017 (SHAttered), so both are unusable for signatures and certificates. SHA-256 and SHA-3 are not collision-broken. A plain hash is also not a password store: that needs a slow KDF plus a per-user salt.

CS::Security.f: Why salt a password, and what does it protect against?
CS::Security.b: A per-user random salt makes identical passwords hash differently, so one rainbow table cannot attack the whole database, and it stops a precomputation working across accounts. With a slow KDF such as Argon2 or scrypt plus a salt, a stolen database is not trivially crackable offline.

CS::Security.f: What is the TLS handshake protecting, and in what order?
CS::Security.b:
1. Client hello with a cipher suite list and a random nonce.
2. Server hello, certificate, and its own nonce.
3. Client verifies the certificate chain against a trusted root and the hostname, then derives the symmetric session keys.
The certificate is the only thing authenticating the server; the nonces are what prevent replay.

CS::Security.f: What is SQL injection, and what prevents it?
CS::Security.b: Building a query by concatenating user input lets an attacker insert SQL syntax, so \(1=1\) or a trailing drop can change the query's meaning. The fix is parameterised queries, where input is bound as data and never parsed as code. Escaping is fragile; binding is not. Object-relational mappers usually parameterise, which is another reason to use them.

CS::Security.f: What is a buffer overflow, and why is it still common?
CS::Security.b: Writing past the end of a buffer into adjacent memory, which can corrupt a pointer or a return address. It persists because C and C++ do not check bounds, and copy functions trust caller lengths. Mitigations: ASLR, stack canaries, and non-executable stacks, which raise the bar rather than removing the bug.

CS::Security.f: What is a race condition-to-privilege escalation in setuid programs?
CS::Security.b: Setuid binaries run with the file owner's privileges, so if such a program operates on a file in a world-writable directory, an attacker can swap the file between the permission check and the use (a TOCTOU bug) and get the privileged code to act on their file. The lesson is that privileged code must do its checks atomically.

CS::ML.f: What is overfitting, and how do you detect it?
CS::ML.b: Fitting the noise in the training set, so training error falls while held-out error rises. It is detected by the gap between training and validation curves, and reduced with more data, regularisation, or simpler models. Testing on data used for tuning is not a held-out estimate.

CS::ML.f: Why is a single train/test split often misleading?
CS::ML.b: One split is one sample, and a lucky split can differ a lot. Use k-fold cross-validation and report the spread across folds, not just the mean. Keep a final test set that is touched once, or the reported number is optimistically biased by model selection.

Underfitting is high bias: the model is too simple to capture the pattern. Overfitting is high variance: it captures noise. Total error is bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise, so the goal is a model complex enough for the signal but not for the noise; validation error is what tells you where you are.

CS::ML.f: What is gradient descent, and what are its two failure modes?
CS::ML.b:
\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\nabla_\theta L(\theta) \]
Fails with too large a step (oscillation or divergence) and too small a step (too slow, and it can stall in a narrow valley rather than a minimum). Adaptive methods such as Adam and RMSProp scale the step per parameter, and momentum and second-order methods handle the valleys.

CS::ML.f: What does the chain rule give for backpropagation?
CS::ML.b: Compute gradients by walking the computational graph backwards, reusing the local derivatives already computed in the forward pass, so each parameter gradient costs one pass. It is exact, not an approximation, and O(params) instead of the exponential cost of symbolic differentiation.

CS::ML.f: What are the layers of a feedforward network for, and what is its universal approximation limit?
CS::ML.b: Layers of affine maps plus a nonlinearity compose nonlinear functions, and a single sufficiently wide hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain. In practice depth matters more than width, and this theorem says nothing about how many samples you need or how hard optimisation is, which is why it overstates the practical result.

CS::ML.f: What is the difference between regularisation methods?
CS::ML.b: L1 (lasso) penalises \(\|\theta\|_1\) and can zero coefficients, giving feature selection. L2 (ridge) penalises \(\|\theta\|_2^2\) and shrinks, staying dense. Both are convex, which is a real advantage. Dropout and early stopping are different in kind: they perturb training rather than constrain the objective.
